rationale: X is at overall parity with the references: it accurately distinguishes Thor's content-aware create behavior from path-based revoke behavior, grounds generator resolution and engine roots in Rails, and treats the alleged inconsistency as an intent question rather than a confirmed defect. It covers every requested CLI case, including migrations as a useful collision boundary, while separating observed source behavior from unverified interactive and end-to-end behavior and avoiding implementation prescriptions. Its proposed `--skip` rule for destroy sits somewhat awkwardly beside its later statement that destroy-after-skip remains open, and it ran no live CLI reproduction, but the references retain the same core ambiguity and do not provide stronger execution evidence.

shortcomings.summary: The desired destroy policy is internally tentative
shortcomings.evidence: The desired-behavior section says `--skip` means neither command changes the existing file, but the destroy-after-skipped-collision example later leaves both keeping and removing that file open; the brief could distinguish the leading hypothesis from the unresolved contract more cleanly.

shortcomings.summary: No end-to-end CLI behavior was executed
shortcomings.evidence: X explicitly says it did not run live generate or destroy commands, so prompt handling, piped EOF, engine-root output, and skip-then-destroy remain inferred from source and existing tests rather than captured as actual command transcripts.

strengths.summary: The technical account matches Rails and Thor
strengths.evidence: Generate and Destroy both call Rails::Generators.invoke with the same destination root but opposite invoke/revoke behavior; Thor reports identical before force or skip on create, prompts on differing content, treats EOF as overwrite, and revoke removes an existing destination without content comparison or collision prompting.

strengths.summary: It covers the requested acceptance matrix comprehensively
strengths.evidence: X addresses identical and differing files, force, skip, yes/no/all/quit, non-interactive stdin, nested mountable-engine roots, namespaced and fallback lookup, missing generators, destroy after a skipped collision, and the ordinary-file versus migration distinction.

strengths.summary: It preserves uncertainty instead of declaring intentional behavior defective
strengths.evidence: X explicitly leaves path-based destroy, destroy-after-skip, EOF overwrite, migration hard errors, destroy flags, and the destroy help pointer as questions requiring public-contract or live-CLI evidence before behavior changes are justified.
